Empirical Research Plan  
“From Portage to Prosperity?  The Long-Run Economic Impact of Early Natural Transportation Routes in the United States”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary strategy: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with dynamic event-study coefficients.

Why DID is appropriate  
• Portage sites are time-invariant, purely geographic features that were highly valuable until ca. 1850 (arrival of rail).  
• We observe the same counties over 20+ census waves (1790-2020).  
• We can compare the evolution of economic outcomes in counties “treated” by a historical portage with otherwise similar river-adjacent counties that never hosted a portage.  
• Because railroads (and later highways) made portage obsolete, treatment intensity effectively “switches off,” giving us differential timing in the importance of the shock which can be captured by period-specific interactions.  
• Event-study coefficients allow us to check pre-trends, estimate persistence/decay, and visualise dynamic effects.

Robustness / complementary designs  
• IV: use the geologically-predicted location of the least-cost break-in-waterway (portage suitability) as an instrument for early market access to verify DID findings.  
• Spatial RDD as an additional check: compare outcomes for observations just inside vs. just outside a 10-km buffer around the historic portage line while forcing a common river corridor.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treated_i = 1 if county centroid lies within 10 km of a documented pre-railroad portage path linking two navigable waterways.

Control group  
River counties without portage: counties whose centroid lies within 10 km of any navigable waterway in 1820 but no recorded portage within 30 km.  
Rationale: ensures comparable water access, climate, soil, and early economic orientation while excluding the specific “break-of-bulk” advantage.

Treatment timing / event date  
We code three eras that map into the DID:

  • Pre-importance (t ≤ 1790): baseline  
  • Portage era (1790–1850): period in which portage conferred a transportation cost advantage  
  • Post-rail era (≥ 1890): period after the advantage disappeared

Implementation: interacted era dummies with the portage indicator to form a staggered DID; the “switch” happens in 1850 when rails reached essentially every portage included in the data.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends in the absence of portage advantage  
   Conditional on water-county fixed effects and baseline covariates, portage and non-portage river counties would have followed the same outcome paths.

Plausibility: river counties share geography; we can inspect pre-1790/1820 outcomes for trend similarity.

A2. No time-varying confounders correlated with both portage status and outcomes after conditioning on county & year FE, river FE, and controls (soil fertility, climate, distance to ocean, elevation, early railroad penetration).  
   Plausible given extensive controls but must be tested.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers).  
   Possible violation if nearby non-portage counties benefited from proximity; we will drop neighbors within 30 km in robustness tests.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Selection on unobservable geography (e.g., fall line, confluences).  
  Mitigation:   
  • Add granular geographic controls (slope, river density, natural harbors, soil suitability).  
  • Matched-pairs design within the same river basin; include river-basin×year FE.

Threat 2: Pre-existing settlement patterns that both caused portage designation and predict modern outcomes.  
  Mitigation:   
  • Include lagged outcomes (population 1790) to soak up initial differences.  
  • Event-study pre-period coefficients to test for differential pre-trends.

Threat 3: Differential arrival and routing of railroads & highways.  
  Mitigation:   
  • Control for distance to 1850 rail network & 1920 Federal-Aid Highway within county.  
  • Placebo DID where “treatment” is early rail access but portage indicator is omitted; check that our main effect survives.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#-------------------------------------------------
# 0.  Libraries
#-------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # data wrangling
library(sf)             # spatial work
library(fixest)         # fast FE regressions
library(MatchIt)        # matching (robustness)

#-------------------------------------------------
# 1.  Load data
#-------------------------------------------------
# counties (with shape)
cnty   <- st_read("input/county_shapes.shp")

# portage lines
port   <- st_read("input/portage_sites.shp")

# navigable rivers 1820
rivers <- st_read("input/navigable_rivers_1820.shp")

# panel of outcomes 1790–2020 (pop density, night-lights, GDP)
panel  <- fread("input/county_panel_1790_2020.csv")

#-------------------------------------------------
# 2.  Construct treatment & control
#-------------------------------------------------
# distance from county centroid to nearest portage
cnty$dist_port <- st_distance(st_centroid(cnty), port) |> as.numeric()

# Treated if ≤10 km
cnty$treated   <- as.integer(cnty$dist_port <= 10000)

# river counties
cnty$dist_riv  <- st_distance(st_centroid(cnty), rivers) |> as.numeric()
cnty$river     <- as.integer(cnty$dist_riv <= 10000)

# Keep water counties
sample <- merge(panel, st_drop_geometry(cnty[,c("GEOID","treated","river")]),
                by = "GEOID")[river == 1]

# Era dummies
sample[, era_port := fifelse(year < 1850, "pre",
                      fifelse(year < 1890, "portage", "post"))]
sample[, port_era := interaction(treated, era_port)]

#-------------------------------------------------
# 3.  Main DID specification
#-------------------------------------------------
spec_main <- feols(outcome ~ i(treated, era_port, ref = "pre") +
                    soil_quality + elevation + dist_ocean +
                    i(year, state) | GEOID + year,  # county & year FE
                    cluster = ~state,
                    data = sample)

etable(spec_main, se = "cluster")

#-------------------------------------------------
# 4.  Dynamic event-study plot
#-------------------------------------------------
event <- feols(outcome ~ sunab(treated, year) +
                soil_quality + elevation |
                GEOID + year,
                cluster = ~state,
                data = sample[year >= 1790 & year <= 1920])

iplot(event)          # pre-trend check

#-------------------------------------------------
# 5.  Robustness: matched sample OLS
#-------------------------------------------------
m <- matchit(treated ~ soil_quality + elevation + dist_ocean,
             data = sample[year==1850], method = "nearest")
matched_ids <- data.table(GEOID = rownames(m$match.matrix))[, matched:=1]
sample <- merge(sample, matched_ids, by = "GEOID", all.x = TRUE)
spec_match <- feols(outcome ~ treated + controls |
                    GEOID + year, data = sample[matched==1])

#-------------------------------------------------
# 6.  Save results
#-------------------------------------------------
saveRDS(list(main = spec_main, event = event, match = spec_match),
        "output/portage_results.rds")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory of path dependence predicts a positive and persistent effect:  
• Portage facilitated early agglomeration, fixed investments, and governmental presence that survived the technology shift.  
Direction: β > 0 for log population density, urban share, per-capita income.  
Magnitude (back-of-the-envelope): treated counties today are ≈ 15–25 percent more populous and 8–12 percent richer per capita than comparable non-portage river counties.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically verified ............... 0.8  
C2: No anticipatory behavior (portage sites pre-exist) .................... 1  
C3: No interference between units (spillovers limited) .................... 0.7  
C4: Exogenous treatment timing (geography + rail cut-off) ................. 0.9  
C5: Stable composition of counties over time (control for boundary changes) 0.8

Average score ≈ 0.84 → credible but not bullet-proof; results must be interpreted with remaining caution.
